Just now

--

Most AI agents are black boxes. You send a message, something happens, and you get a response. But what happened? Which tool actually ran? How many tokens did that burn? Was the slowdown coming from the LLM or the vector store?
I’d been sitting with this problem for a while — LangGraph gives you a state machine, not visibility into it. Then the Agents of SigNoz Hackathon landed: one week, one constraint, build something that actually uses SigNoz. That was the push I needed. So I built AgentLens — an agentic RAG system where nothing hides. Every decision, every token, every tool call traced and visible in real time.
This is the honest version of how I built it. What worked, what broke, and what I’d do differently.
What I Built
AgentLens is a conversational AI agent — but the interesting part isn’t what it does, it’s how much you can see while it’s doing it.
Under the hood:

• A LangGraph ReAct graph — written manually, not the prebuilt shortcut

• Dual-layer memory: short-term through LangGraph checkpointing, long-term through Postgres

• RAG pipeline backed by Pinecone for document search

• 6 tools: web search, weather, finance, datetime, calculator, and document search

• Full OpenTelemetry instrumentation piping into SigNoz Cloud

• A live observability sidebar in the React frontend that updates while the agent is still responding
Here’s the part I’m most proud of: the agent is observable from both sides using the same identifier. The frontend sidebar shows a session ID. That same ID is the session.id attribute on the root span in SigNoz. Grab it, drop it into Trace Explorer, and you're looking at the exact trace for that conversation — no searching, no guessing.
Under the hood, the agent exposes its own metrics through a /metrics/session/{session_id} endpoint that the frontend polls every 2 seconds during a stream. It's not magic — but it feels like it when it works.
The agent is observable from both sides — using the same identifier. That’s not a coincidence, that was the whole point.

The First Real Problem: Auto-Instrumentation Broke on Render
My original plan was straightforward. Use openinference-instrumentation-langchain — the standard auto-instrumentation library for LangChain/LangGraph — and let it handle the spans. It worked fine locally on my Windows machine.
Then I pushed to Render.
Render runs Python 3.14. The library caps out at 3.12. Every deployment crashed at startup with an import error. I spent two hours hunting for a compatible version before accepting that it wasn’t going to happen.
So I made a call: rip the library out and write every span by hand.
It felt like the harder path at the time. It wasn’t. Manual instrumentation meant I controlled exactly what got traced, how it got named, and what attributes landed on each span. The auto-instrumentation would’ve given me something — but not this.
Once I committed to manual instrumentation, this is what it actually looked like:
# telemetry.py — manual tracer setup
_tracer = trace.get_tracer(“agentlens.reasoner”)
# Inside reasoner.py
with _tracer.start_as_current_span(“agentlens.reasoner”) as span:
span.set_attribute(“llm.model”, “gemini-3.1-flash-lite”)
span.set_attribute(“llm.message_count”, len(messages))
t0 = time.perf_counter()
response = await llm_with_tools.ainvoke(messages)
latency_ms = (time.perf_counter() — t0) * 1000
span.set_attribute(“llm.input_tokens”, input_tokens)
span.set_attribute(“llm.output_tokens”, output_tokens)
span.set_attribute(“llm.latency_ms”, round(latency_ms, 2))
Auto-instrumentation gives you generic spans. Manual spans give you exactly the attributes you care about. The constraint forced a better decision.
Instrumenting Every Layer
I ended up with 11 custom span types — one for each operation that actually matters inside the agent.
agentlens.chat.stream — the root span for an entire conversation turn. Every trace in SigNoz is tagged with session.id and user.id, so nothing gets lost in the noise.
agentlens.reasoner — fires on every LLM call. Tracks token counts (input, output, total), latency, and how many tool calls the model requested.
agentlens.tool.<name> — one child span per tool invocation. Logs the tool name, what went in, a preview of what came out, how long it took, and whether it succeeded or failed.
agentlens.ltm.read / agentlens.ltm.write — wraps every long-term memory read and write. Captures the operation type, the key being touched, and record count.
agentlens.rag.query — wraps every vector store query across both ChromaDB locally and Pinecone in prod. Logs the backend, results returned, latency, and similarity threshold.
By the end, nothing in the agent runs without leaving a trace. That was the goal.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

In SigNoz, this turns into a clean waterfall for every single chat message:
agentlens.chat.stream [2.98s]
├── agentlens.ltm.read [12ms]
├── agentlens.reasoner [890ms]
│ └── ChatGoogleGenerativeAI [850ms]
├── agentlens.tool.get_datetime [3ms]
└── agentlens.reasoner [1155ms]
At a glance you can see the full turn took 2.98 seconds. The LLM decided it needed the datetime tool, called it in 3ms, then made a second reasoning pass to form the final response. The long-term memory read happened before any of that — 12ms, barely noticeable.
This is what observability actually looks like when it’s working. Not a log file you grep through after something breaks. A timeline you read in real time.

The Second Real Problem: The Parent Span Kept Disappearing
I lost half a day to this one.
agentlens.chat.stream wasn't showing up in SigNoz — but all the child spans were there. The trace existed, the root span didn't. That's a specific kind of confusing.
The root cause was subtle. stream_agent_response is an async generator — it uses yield to stream SSE events to the frontend. I'd opened the parent span inside that generator with a with block:
# This was wrong
async def stream_agent_response(…) -> AsyncGenerator[str, None]:
with _tracer.start_as_current_span(“agentlens.chat.stream”) as span:
async for event in graph.astream_events(…):
yield format_sse(event) # span stays open across yields
The problem: async generators hold spans open across yield points. The span only exports when the generator is fully exhausted. On Render — with network latency and free tier sleep behavior — the generator was sometimes garbage collected before the OTLP exporter could flush. Span dropped. No trace.
The fix was to pull the span out of the generator entirely:
# Correct — span lives in a regular async function, not the generator
async def stream_agent_response(…) -> AsyncGenerator[str, None]:
span = _tracer.start_span(“agentlens.chat.stream”)
span.set_attribute(“session.id”, thread_id)
with trace.use_span(span, end_on_exit=True):
ctx = otel_context.get_current()
# Pass captured context to the inner generator
async for chunk in _stream_events(…, ctx):
yield chunk
async def _stream_events(…, ctx):
token = otel_context.attach(ctx)
try:
# actual streaming logic here
…
finally:
otel_context.detach(token)
The span now opens and closes inside a regular async function — not a generator — so it exports reliably. The inner generator gets the captured OTel context passed in explicitly, so child spans still attach correctly under the root.
Once I understood the problem, the fix took 20 minutes. Finding it took four hours.
6 Custom Metrics in SigNoz
Traces tell you what happened. Metrics tell you how the system is behaving over time. I wanted both.
I registered 6 custom metric instruments in telemetry.py:
meter = metrics.get_meter(“agentlens.metrics”)
token_cost_counter = meter.create_counter(
name=”agentlens.tokens.total”,
description=”Total tokens consumed across all LLM calls”,
unit=”tokens”,
)
retrieval_latency_histogram = meter.create_histogram(
name=”agentlens.retrieval.latency”,
description=”Vector store retrieval latency in milliseconds”,
unit=”ms”,
)
active_sessions_gauge = meter.create_up_down_counter(
name=”agentlens.sessions.active”,
description=”Number of currently active chat sessions”,
unit=”sessions”,
)
All 6 are live and confirmed flowing into SigNoz Cloud from production.
On top of that, I built a custom “AgentLens Observability” dashboard in SigNoz with 4 panels: Token Usage Over Time, LLM Latency P99, Tool Invocations, and Memory Operations. Not a screenshot for the README — an actual dashboard I use to watch the system run.

Alerts That Actually Fire
I set up two alerts in SigNoz:

• High RAG Retrieval Latency — triggers when agentlens.retrieval.latency p99 crosses 2000ms over a 5-minute window

• Token Cost Spike — triggers when agentlens.tokens.total sum exceeds 500 tokens in 5 minutes
Both fired during development. Both sent email notifications.
There’s something genuinely strange about getting an alert on your phone because your own hackathon project is misbehaving. But that’s exactly the point — if the observability only works when nothing’s wrong, it’s not observability.

The Self-Awareness Layer
Most observability setups have one consumer: the monitoring backend. AgentLens has two.
Every instrumented call writes to SigNoz and to an in-memory session store simultaneously:
# Same instrumentation, two consumers
tel.token_cost_counter.add(total_tokens, {“llm.model”: model}) # → SigNoz
tel.record_session_tokens(session_id, input_tokens, output_tokens, latency_ms) # → session store
The GET /metrics/session/{session_id} endpoint aggregates that session store and returns:
{
“tokens”: { “input”: 3406, “output”: 28, “total”: 3434 },
“llm”: { “calls”: 2, “last_latency_ms”: 916.19 },
“tools”: { “total_calls”: 1, “calls”: [{ “name”: “get_datetime”, “latency_ms”: 3.0 }] },
“session”: { “duration_seconds”: 2.98 }
}
The React frontend polls this every 2 seconds and renders it live in a sidebar — while the agent is still responding.
The session ID in that sidebar is the same session.id attribute on the root span in SigNoz. That's the bridge: a user watching the frontend and an engineer watching SigNoz are looking at the same conversation through two different lenses, connected by a single identifier.
That’s what I mean when I call it self-aware. It’s not just observable from the outside — it exposes itself from the inside too.
What I Learned
Manual instrumentation beats auto-instrumentation for agents. Auto-instrumentation gives you generic HTTP spans. Manual gives you exactly what you care about — token counts, tool latency, retrieval results. The constraint that forced my hand ended up producing better observability than the easy path would have.
Async generators and spans don’t mix. If you’re using SSE or any streaming pattern, never open a span inside a generator. The span lifecycle and the generator lifecycle don’t align. Separate them explicitly — I learned this the hard way.
The three OTel signals are a complete picture, not three versions of the same thing. Metrics tell you something is wrong. Traces show you where. Logs tell you why. All three flowing together with correlated trace IDs is when observability stops being data collection and starts being actually useful.
Observability is an architecture decision, not a feature you add later. I could have bolted SigNoz on at the end. Instead the session store, the metrics endpoint, and the frontend panel were built as first-class features from the start. That’s what made everything else possible.
